Core sample CS-01 · 2,600 to 2,850 ft

Contracts come with short notice and the longest parts take months. How far ahead can the rig count be forecast well enough to act on?

Method
Time-series forecasting (ARIMA, ETS)
Data
US rotary rig count, monthly (EIA, from Baker Hughes)
R packages
forecast, tidyverse, readxl

``` ::::: {.cs-sec} :::: {.num} 01 :::: :::: {} ## Project overview Work in downhole tools can arrive with little notice, while the longest parts take months to come in. I tested how far ahead the US rig count, the most watched measure of drilling activity, can be forecast well enough to act on. The answer is about one quarter. Out to three months, an ARIMA model misses by about a third less than simply assuming no change. By six months most of that edge is gone, and past eight months the model does no better than assuming no change at all. It also missed both big turns, in late 2014 and early 2020. So I'd use the forecast as a monthly check on whether to get ready, by refreshing quotes and asking shops about capacity. I would not use it to decide how much to buy. The bill of materials does that. :::: ::::: ::::: {.cs-sec} :::: {.num} 02 :::: :::: {} ## Problem statement In the build-to-order work I've done, parts are bought off the bill of materials once a contract is signed. A forecast can't tell a buyer how many parts to order, and I wouldn't use one for that. The trouble is timing. A contract can land with days or weeks of notice, and the longest parts take months to arrive. Any early sign that work is picking up is worth having, because it tells a buyer when to refresh quotes and ask shops about capacity before the rush. The rig count is the most watched measure of drilling activity. So the question is: **how far ahead can the rig count be forecast well enough to act on, and how would a buyer know when to trust it?** One limit up front. Whether more rigs means more tool orders, and how soon, is an assumption here. I have no public data that ties the two together. :::: ::::: ::::: {.cs-sec} :::: {.num} 03 :::: :::: {} ## Approach ### Step 1 · Get the data and look at all of it Baker Hughes counts the rotary rigs drilling in the US every week. The Energy Information Administration republishes that count as a monthly average going back to 1973, in one file with a fixed address. I used the EIA file so anyone can rerun this. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(dplyr) library(tidyr) library(ggplot2) library(scales) library(readxl) library(forecast) library(knitr) # The site's chart style. bp_both() draws each chart twice: # once for the light sheet and once for the dark print. source("_blueprint.R") bp_device() # One workbook, one sheet per breakdown. The first two rows are EIA's own labels. eia <- "data/NG_ENR_DRILL_S1_M.xls" rigs <- read_excel(eia, sheet = "Data 1", skip = 2) names(rigs) <- c("date", "rigs") type <- read_excel(eia, sheet = "Data 3", skip = 2) names(type) <- c("date", "Oil", "Gas") rigs$date <- as.Date(rigs$date) type$date <- as.Date(type$date) peak <- rigs[which.max(rigs$rigs), ] trough <- rigs[which.min(rigs$rigs), ] latest <- rigs[nrow(rigs), ] ``` ::: ::: {.cell renderings='["light","dark"]'} ```{.r .cell-code} # Three points worth naming, each with a spot for its label that is clear of the line marks <- bind_rows( data.frame(peak, label = paste0(format(peak$date, "%b %Y"), ": ", comma(peak$rigs)), lx = peak$date + 400, ly = peak$rigs, hjust = 0), data.frame(trough, label = paste0(format(trough$date, "%b %Y"), ": ", trough$rigs), lx = trough$date - 400, ly = 120, hjust = 1), data.frame(latest, label = paste0(format(latest$date, "%b %Y"), ": ", latest$rigs), lx = latest$date, ly = 1150, hjust = 1)) bp_both(function(k) { ggplot(rigs, aes(date, rigs)) + annotate("rect", xmin = as.Date("2000-01-01"), xmax = max(rigs$date), ymin = 0, ymax = Inf, fill = k$mark, alpha = 0.08) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.7, colour = k$mark) + geom_segment(data = marks[3, ], aes(xend = date, y = rigs + 60, yend = ly - 90), linewidth = 0.3, colour = k$ink) + geom_point(data = marks, size = 2.2, colour = k$ink) + geom_text(data = marks, aes(x = lx, y = ly, label = label, hjust = hjust), size = 3.4, colour = k$ink) + annotate("text", x = as.Date("2000-06-01"), y = 4350, label = "Modeled from 2000", hjust = 0, size = 3.2, colour = k$ink3) + scale_y_continuous(labels = comma, limits = c(0, 4700), expand = c(0, 0)) + scale_x_date(date_breaks = "10 years", date_labels = "%Y") + labs(title = "The rig count has no normal level. It moves in long, steep swings.", subtitle = paste0("The ", format(peak$date, "%Y"), " peak was ", round(peak$rigs / trough$rigs), " times the ", format(trough$date, "%Y"), " low."), x = NULL, y = "Rigs in operation") }) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Fig. 1 · US rotary rigs in operation, monthly average, 1973 to 2026. The shaded span is the part the models learn from.](rig-count_files/figure-html/chart-history-1.png){fig-alt='Line chart of the US rig count since 1973. It peaks above 4,500 in late 1981, falls for two decades, swings between 400 and 2,000 after 2000, and hits its low of 250 in August 2020.' width=768} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Fig. 1 · US rotary rigs in operation, monthly average, 1973 to 2026. The shaded span is the part the models learn from.](rig-count_files/figure-html/chart-history-2.png){fig-alt='Line chart of the US rig count since 1973. It peaks above 4,500 in late 1981, falls for two decades, swings between 400 and 2,000 after 2000, and hits its low of 250 in August 2020.' width=768} ::: ::: The count has been as high as 4,521 and as low as 250. The 1970s and 1980s were a different industry, so I modeled from 2000 on. ::: {.cell renderings='["light","dark"]'} ```{.r .cell-code} by_type <- type %>% filter(!is.na(Oil)) %>% pivot_longer(c(Oil, Gas), names_to = "target", values_to = "rigs") %>% mutate(target = factor(target, levels = c("Oil", "Gas"))) crossover <- max(type$date[which(type$Gas > type$Oil)]) # last month gas rigs led ends <- by_type %>% filter(date == max(date)) bp_both(function(k) { ggplot(by_type, aes(date, rigs, colour = target)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) + geom_text(data = ends, aes(label = paste0(target, " ", rigs)), hjust = -0.12, size = 3.4, colour = k$ink) + scale_colour_manual(values = setNames(k$series[1:2], c("Oil", "Gas"))) + scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) + scale_x_date(date_breaks = "5 years", date_labels = "%Y", expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.16))) + labs(title = "Gas rigs led until 2011. Oil has led ever since.", subtitle = "What the rigs drill for changed, which is one more reason to model recent years only.", x = NULL, y = "Rigs in operation") + theme(legend.position = "none") }) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Fig. 2 · Rigs drilling for oil and for natural gas, monthly, since the split was first reported in 1987](rig-count_files/figure-html/chart-type-1.png){fig-alt='Two lines. Gas rigs outnumber oil rigs from the mid 1990s until 2011. After that oil rigs lead by a wide margin.' width=768} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Fig. 2 · Rigs drilling for oil and for natural gas, monthly, since the split was first reported in 1987](rig-count_files/figure-html/chart-type-2.png){fig-alt='Two lines. Gas rigs outnumber oil rigs from the mid 1990s until 2011. After that oil rigs lead by a wide margin.' width=768} ::: ::: ### Step 2 · Check for a season A forecast usually starts by pulling out the season. Before modeling one, I checked whether there is one. ::: {.cell renderings='["light","dark"]'} ```{.r .cell-code} recent <- rigs %>% filter(date >= as.Date("2000-01-01")) change <- recent %>% mutate(pct = (rigs / lag(rigs) - 1) * 100, last_pct = lag(pct), month = factor(format(date, "%b"), levels = month.abb)) %>% filter(!is.na(last_pct)) season_test <- kruskal.test(pct ~ month, data = change) bp_both(function(k) { ggplot(change, aes(month, pct)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.4, colour = k$ink) + geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.6, outlier.alpha = 0.4, linewidth = 0.5, colour = k$mark, fill = NA, width = 0.6) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-12, 12)) + scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) + labs(title = "No calendar month stands out, so there is no season to model", x = NULL, y = "Change from the month before") + theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()) }) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Fig. 3 · Month-to-month change in the rig count, by calendar month, 2000 to 2026. The few changes beyond 12% are cut off.](rig-count_files/figure-html/chart-season-1.png){fig-alt='Twelve box plots, one per calendar month. All twelve boxes sit close to zero and overlap heavily.' width=768} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Fig. 3 · Month-to-month change in the rig count, by calendar month, 2000 to 2026. The few changes beyond 12% are cut off.](rig-count_files/figure-html/chart-season-2.png){fig-alt='Twelve box plots, one per calendar month. All twelve boxes sit close to zero and overlap heavily.' width=768} ::: ::: A Kruskal-Wallis test finds no difference between calendar months (p = 0.65). US drilling doesn't stop for winter, so I left the season out of both models. ### Step 3 · Find what a model can use With no season, the question is what pattern is left. The answer is momentum. ::: {.cell renderings='["light","dark"]'} ```{.r .cell-code} momentum <- cor(change$pct, change$last_pct) bp_both(function(k) { ggplot(change, aes(last_pct, pct)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3, colour = k$axis) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3, colour = k$axis) + geom_point(alpha = 0.55, size = 1.5, stroke = 0) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.8, colour = k$ink) + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-20, 15), ylim = c(-20, 15)) + scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) + scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) + labs(title = "A rising count tends to keep rising, and a falling one keeps falling", subtitle = "Each dot is one month. Three months in 2020 fell further than the chart shows.", x = "Change the month before", y = "Change this month") }) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Fig. 4 · Each month's change in the rig count against the change the month before, 2000 to 2026](rig-count_files/figure-html/chart-momentum-1.png){fig-alt='Scatter plot. Points run from lower left to upper right along a clear line: a month that follows a rise tends to rise, and a month that follows a fall tends to fall.' width=768} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Fig. 4 · Each month's change in the rig count against the change the month before, 2000 to 2026](rig-count_files/figure-html/chart-momentum-2.png){fig-alt='Scatter plot. Points run from lower left to upper right along a clear line: a month that follows a rise tends to rise, and a month that follows a fall tends to fall.' width=768} ::: ::: The correlation is 0.81. Rigs are contracted and moved over months, so a turn takes time to play out. That lag is the one thing a model of the count alone can learn. ### Step 4 · Fit the models and hold back a year I fit two standard models and one yardstick to the data through August 2025, then forecast the twelve months they had not seen. - **ARIMA.** Predicts next month's change from this month's change and last month's miss. It is built for momentum. - **ETS** (exponential smoothing). Tracks a level and a trend, and weights recent months most. - **No change.** Next month equals this month. Any model has to beat this to be worth running. Both models work on the log of the count. That keeps their ranges above zero and makes a miss of 50 rigs count for more at 500 rigs than at 2,000. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dates <- recent$date y <- ts(recent$rigs, start = c(2000, 1), frequency = 12) h <- 12 # forecast twelve months ahead train <- head(y, length(y) - h) test <- tail(y, h) fit_arima <- auto.arima(train, lambda = 0, seasonal = FALSE) # lambda = 0 models the log fit_ets <- ets(train, lambda = 0) held <- list(`No change` = naive(train, h = h, lambda = 0), ETS = forecast(fit_ets, h = h), ARIMA = forecast(fit_arima, h = h)) held_scores <- bind_rows(lapply(names(held), function(m) { a <- accuracy(held[[m]], test)["Test set", ] data.frame(Model = m, `Average miss` = paste0(round(a["MAPE"], 1), "%"), `Average miss, rigs` = round(a["MAE"]), check.names = FALSE) })) kable(held_scores, align = "lrr", row.names = FALSE, caption = "Accuracy on the twelve held-back months") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: Accuracy on the twelve held-back months |Model | Average miss| Average miss, rigs| |:---------|------------:|------------------:| |No change | 3.1%| 18| |ETS | 6.5%| 37| |ARIMA | 3.1%| 18| ::: ::: ::: {.cell renderings='["light","dark"]'} ```{.r .cell-code} test_dates <- tail(dates, h) held_lines <- bind_rows(lapply(names(held), function(m) data.frame(method = m, date = test_dates, rigs = as.numeric(held[[m]]$mean)))) %>% mutate(method = factor(method, levels = c("ARIMA", "ETS", "No change"))) context <- recent %>% filter(date >= as.Date("2024-01-01")) bp_both(function(k) { ggplot(held_lines, aes(date, rigs)) + annotate("rect", xmin = min(test_dates) - 15, xmax = max(test_dates) + 15, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = k$mark, alpha = 0.08) + geom_line(data = context, linewidth = 0.9, colour = k$ink) + geom_line(aes(colour = method, linetype = method), linewidth = 0.9) + annotate("text", x = min(test_dates), y = 632, label = "Held back", hjust = 0, size = 3.2, colour = k$ink3) + scale_colour_manual(values = c(ARIMA = k$series[1], ETS = k$series[2], `No change` = k$ink3)) + scale_linetype_manual(values = c(ARIMA = "solid", ETS = "solid", `No change` = "22")) + scale_x_date(date_breaks = "6 months", date_labels = "%b %Y") + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(480, 640)) + labs(title = "On a quiet year, assuming no change was as good as anything", subtitle = "The solid dark line is the actual count.", x = NULL, y = "Rigs in operation") + theme(legend.key.width = unit(1.4, "cm")) }) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Fig. 5 · The held-back year: what each method forecast, and what the rig count did](rig-count_files/figure-html/chart-held-1.png){fig-alt='Line chart. The actual count stays near 545 for most of the year and rises to 589 at the end. The ARIMA and no-change forecasts are flat at 538. The ETS forecast drifts down to about 500.' width=768} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Fig. 5 · The held-back year: what each method forecast, and what the rig count did](rig-count_files/figure-html/chart-held-2.png){fig-alt='Line chart. The actual count stays near 545 for most of the year and rises to 589 at the end. The ARIMA and no-change forecasts are flat at 538. The ETS forecast drifts down to about 500.' width=768} ::: ::: The model R chose is ARIMA(1,1,1), a plain momentum model. On this one year it tied with assuming no change, and ETS did worse because it carried an old downward trend forward. One quiet year proves little, though. It says nothing about the years that hurt. ### Step 5 · Replay sixteen years of forecasts So I replayed history. For every month from December 2009 on, I gave each method only the data known that month, had it forecast the next twelve, and scored it against what came after. That is 200 forecasts per method, through booms, two crashes, and long flat spells. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} replay_one <- function(o) { known <- ts(y[1:o], start = start(y), frequency = 12) f <- list(`No change` = naive(known, h = h, lambda = 0, level = 80), ETS = forecast(ets(known, lambda = 0), h = h, level = 80), ARIMA = forecast(auto.arima(known, lambda = 0, seasonal = FALSE), h = h, level = 80)) bind_rows(lapply(names(f), function(m) data.frame( origin = o, method = m, ahead = 1:h, today = y[o], forecast = as.numeric(f[[m]]$mean), low = as.numeric(f[[m]]$lower), # the 80% range high = as.numeric(f[[m]]$upper), actual = as.numeric(y[o + 1:h])))) # NA where the future isn't known yet } first_origin <- which(dates == as.Date("2009-12-15")) replay <- bind_rows(lapply(first_origin:length(y), replay_one)) scored <- replay %>% filter(!is.na(actual)) %>% mutate(miss = abs(forecast - actual) / actual * 100, inside = actual >= low & actual <= high) by_ahead <- scored %>% group_by(method, ahead) %>% summarise(typical_miss = median(miss), average_miss = mean(miss), range_held = mean(inside) * 100, .groups = "drop") # The model's edge: how much smaller its typical miss is than "no change" edge <- by_ahead %>% select(method, ahead, typical_miss) %>% pivot_wider(names_from = method, values_from = typical_miss) %>% mutate(arima_edge = (1 - ARIMA / `No change`) * 100, ets_edge = (1 - ETS / `No change`) * 100) ``` ::: ::: {.cell renderings='["light","dark"]'} ```{.r .cell-code} by_ahead <- by_ahead %>% mutate(method = factor(method, levels = c("ARIMA", "ETS", "No change"))) bp_both(function(k) { ggplot(by_ahead, aes(ahead, typical_miss, colour = method, linetype = method)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) + geom_point(size = 1.6) + scale_colour_manual(values = c(ARIMA = k$series[1], ETS = k$series[2], `No change` = k$ink3)) + scale_linetype_manual(values = c(ARIMA = "solid", ETS = "solid", `No change` = "22")) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12) + scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%"), limits = c(0, NA)) + labs(title = "The models earn their keep for about a quarter, then the edge fades", subtitle = "Below the dashed line, a model beats assuming no change.", x = "Months ahead", y = "Typical miss") + theme(legend.key.width = unit(1.4, "cm"), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()) }) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Fig. 6 · Typical miss by how far ahead the forecast looks, from the sixteen-year replay. The typical miss is the median: half of forecasts did better, half did worse.](rig-count_files/figure-html/chart-ahead-1.png){fig-alt='Three rising lines. ARIMA and ETS sit well below the no-change line for the first five months, close the gap by month seven, and cross above it after month eight.' width=768} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Fig. 6 · Typical miss by how far ahead the forecast looks, from the sixteen-year replay. The typical miss is the median: half of forecasts did better, half did worse.](rig-count_files/figure-html/chart-ahead-2.png){fig-alt='Three rising lines. ARIMA and ETS sit well below the no-change line for the first five months, close the gap by month seven, and cross above it after month eight.' width=768} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} by_ahead %>% filter(ahead %in% c(1, 3, 6, 9, 12)) %>% select(method, ahead, typical_miss) %>% pivot_wider(names_from = method, values_from = typical_miss) %>% left_join(edge %>% select(ahead, arima_edge), by = "ahead") %>% left_join(by_ahead %>% filter(method == "ARIMA") %>% select(ahead, range_held), by = "ahead") %>% transmute(`Months ahead` = ahead, `No change` = paste0(round(`No change`, 1), "%"), ETS = paste0(round(ETS, 1), "%"), ARIMA = paste0(round(ARIMA, 1), "%"), `ARIMA's edge` = ifelse(arima_edge > 0, paste0(round(arima_edge), "% smaller"), paste0(round(-arima_edge), "% larger")), `ARIMA's 80% range held` = paste0(round(range_held), "%")) %>% kable(align = "rrrrrr", caption = "Typical miss by distance, and how often the forecast range held") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: Typical miss by distance, and how often the forecast range held | Months ahead| No change| ETS| ARIMA| ARIMA's edge| ARIMA's 80% range held| |------------:|---------:|-----:|-----:|------------:|----------------------:| | 1| 1.6%| 1.2%| 1.1%| 33% smaller| 90%| | 3| 5.6%| 3.3%| 3.5%| 38% smaller| 88%| | 6| 9.3%| 7.9%| 7.8%| 16% smaller| 83%| | 9| 12.2%| 13.1%| 12.9%| 6% larger| 78%| | 12| 17.3%| 19.4%| 19.1%| 11% larger| 75%| ::: ::: Two things stand out. The first is how fast the edge fades. The second is the gap between the typical miss and the average miss: at six months ARIMA's typical miss is 7.8%, but its average miss is 19.1%. A few huge misses pull the average up, and they all sit at the turns. The forecast made in February 2020 for six months later was 821 rigs. The count came in at 250. :::: ::::: ::::: {.cs-sec} :::: {.num} 04 :::: :::: {} ## Results and impact ### When to trust it A forecast is easier to act on as a call than as a number. So I turned each forecast into one: **up** when the whole 80% range sits above today's count, **down** when the whole range sits below it, and **no call** otherwise. Then I checked the calls against what happened. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} calls <- scored %>% filter(method != "No change") %>% mutate(call = case_when(low > today ~ "Up", high < today ~ "Down", TRUE ~ "No call"), right = (call == "Up" & actual > today) | (call == "Down" & actual < today)) call_table <- calls %>% filter(ahead %in% c(3, 6, 9, 12)) %>% group_by(method, ahead) %>% summarise(months = n(), made = sum(call != "No call"), right = sum(right[call != "No call"]), .groups = "drop") call_table %>% arrange(desc(method), ahead) %>% transmute(Model = method, `Months ahead` = ahead, `Calls made` = paste0(made, " of ", months, " months"), `Calls that were right` = paste0(right, " of ", made, " (", round(right / made * 100), "%)")) %>% kable(align = "lrrr", caption = "How often each model made a call, and how often the call was right") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: How often each model made a call, and how often the call was right |Model | Months ahead| Calls made| Calls that were right| |:-----|------------:|----------------:|---------------------:| |ETS | 3| 32 of 198 months| 29 of 32 (91%)| |ETS | 6| 24 of 195 months| 20 of 24 (83%)| |ETS | 9| 16 of 192 months| 11 of 16 (69%)| |ETS | 12| 11 of 189 months| 7 of 11 (64%)| |ARIMA | 3| 26 of 198 months| 22 of 26 (85%)| |ARIMA | 6| 14 of 195 months| 8 of 14 (57%)| |ARIMA | 9| 12 of 192 months| 4 of 12 (33%)| |ARIMA | 12| 9 of 189 months| 1 of 9 (11%)| ::: ::: Both models stay quiet most months, which is honest: most months, the range includes "about the same." Three months out, the calls hold up. ARIMA was right 22 times out of 26, and ETS 29 out of 32. Past a quarter the two models part ways. At six months ARIMA was right 8 times out of 14, which is close to a coin toss, while ETS was right 20 times out of 24. At most two dozen calls in sixteen years is thin evidence, and the models disagree. So I'd treat a call past a quarter as a hint, not a signal. ### The forecast today ::: {.cell renderings='["light","dark"]'} ```{.r .cell-code} fit_now <- auto.arima(y, lambda = 0, seasonal = FALSE) fc_now <- forecast(fit_now, h = h, level = c(80, 95)) future <- seq(max(dates), by = "month", length.out = h + 1)[-1] fan <- data.frame(date = future, forecast = as.numeric(fc_now$mean), low80 = as.numeric(fc_now$lower[, 1]), high80 = as.numeric(fc_now$upper[, 1]), low95 = as.numeric(fc_now$lower[, 2]), high95 = as.numeric(fc_now$upper[, 2])) # Start the bands at the last known point so the fan opens from it anchor <- data.frame(date = max(dates), forecast = latest$rigs, low80 = latest$rigs, high80 = latest$rigs, low95 = latest$rigs, high95 = latest$rigs) fan_plot <- bind_rows(anchor, fan) since <- recent %>% filter(date >= as.Date("2022-01-01")) bp_both(function(k) { ggplot(fan_plot, aes(date)) + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = low95, ymax = high95), fill = k$mark, alpha = 0.14) + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = low80, ymax = high80), fill = k$mark, alpha = 0.24) + geom_line(data = since, aes(y = rigs), linewidth = 0.9, colour = k$ink) + geom_line(aes(y = forecast), linewidth = 0.9, linetype = "42", colour = k$mark) + scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%b %Y") + scale_y_continuous(labels = comma, limits = c(0, NA)) + labs(title = "The range is tight for a month or two, then too wide to act on", x = NULL, y = "Rigs in operation") }) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Fig. 7 · The ARIMA forecast from the latest month of data. The darker band is the 80% range and the lighter band the 95% range.](rig-count_files/figure-html/chart-forecast-1.png){fig-alt='Line chart of the rig count since 2022 with a forecast for the next twelve months. The forecast line is flat near 580. The range around it widens quickly, from about 560 to 610 next month to about 350 to 950 a year out.' width=768} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Fig. 7 · The ARIMA forecast from the latest month of data. The darker band is the 80% range and the lighter band the 95% range.](rig-count_files/figure-html/chart-forecast-2.png){fig-alt='Line chart of the rig count since 2022 with a forecast for the next twelve months. The forecast line is flat near 580. The range around it widens quickly, from about 560 to 610 next month to about 350 to 950 a year out.' width=768} ::: ::: I use ARIMA here and in the replay tool. The two models were close on typical miss, ARIMA is the simpler one, and its ranges stay narrow enough to read. A year out, its 80% range runs from 351 to 953 rigs. The ETS range for the same month runs from 200 to 2,044. From 589 rigs in August 2026, the model expects about 581 three months out, with an 80% range of 501 to 674. That range includes today's count, so the call is: no call. Six months out the range is 433 to 775, too wide to act on. ### What I'd tell a buyer 1. **Run it as a monthly check.** It takes a minute once the new count is out, and most months it will say "no call." That is the right answer most months. 2. **Act on a call only inside a quarter.** A three-month call has been right at least five times in six, whichever model made it. Use it to refresh quotes that are about to expire and to ask shops how full they are, on parts that take a quarter or less. 3. **Don't lean on it for the longest parts.** A part that takes six months needs a six-month view. At that distance neither model beats "no change" by much, and the two disagree on which way to call it. That gap has to be closed some other way, with stock, reserved shop time, or supplier agreements. Those are business decisions a forecast can't make. 4. **Never size an order with it.** It says which way activity is heading. The bill of materials says what to buy. ### What this doesn't settle The model only knows the count's own past, so it will always be late at a turn. Oil prices tend to move before rigs do, and the next thing I'd test is whether adding them stretches the useful range past a quarter. And as said at the start, the step from rig count to tool orders is an assumption I can't check with public data. ::: {#try-it .try-it} [Try it · Replay the forecast]{.label .label-orange} Stand at any month since 2009 and see what the model forecast with only the data it had then.
